d.title: ALL and ANY, and the empty-set behaviour nobody tests for
d.caption: **Both quantifiers read nicely and both have a MAX or MIN equivalent that is usually clearer** — and the reason to prefer the aggregate form is the last two rows. Against an empty set, greater-than-ALL is *trivially true* because there is nothing to fail against, so a filter that should match nobody matches everybody. The MAX form returns NULL instead and the predicate is simply false. **A derived table is the other half of this section:** computing the department averages once as a relation is how an aggregate becomes something you can join to, and it is still the right tool when the aggregate's grain is not the row's.

d.title: One recursion, four questions, and only the anchor and the join direction change
d.caption: **The shape of a recursive CTE never changes — what changes is where you start and which way the join points.** Anchor at a node and join child-to-parent and you walk *down* into a subtree. Anchor at a leaf and join the other way and you climb *up* to the root, which is the chain of command. **The fourth row is the one worth learning:** anchor on every row at once and carry the root's id along, and each employee appears once per ancestor — so grouping by that root gives every manager their subtree payroll in a single pass. That is a bill-of-materials rollup wearing an org chart.

d.title: Rows that exist in no table, and the one line that stops it
d.caption: **A recursive CTE can manufacture rows: start with one value, add an interval each round, and stop when the guard fails.** That is the date spine from lesson 1.5 for engines without generate_series — MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server — and the same three lines generate integers, months, or any arithmetic sequence. **The guard is not optional and it lives in the recursive member's WHERE, not in the outer query:** an outer LIMIT does not stop the recursion, it just stops reading. SQL Server caps the rounds at 100 by default, which turns a forgotten guard into an error rather than a runaway.

d.title: Two index types, and each one only serves its own predicate shape
d.caption: **The last column is the point of the section: an index that exists is not an index that is used.** An expression index is built on one exact expression, so a query written with the JSON-returning arrow instead of the text-returning one misses it entirely — same field, same value, full scan. **A GIN index serves containment and key-existence across any field, and does nothing for a plain text-arrow equality.** So the choice is not which index is better: it is which shape of predicate your code actually writes, and then making the two match.
